assessments.explanation: The abstract reports that DNA methylation in human cerebral cortex changes across the lifespan, with age-related methylation increases at neurogenesis-related genes (NEUROD1, NEUROD2) that track with declining mRNA levels. This supports the link between epigenetic changes in the brain, normal aging, and neurogenesis-related genes. However, the evidence is observational: the study measures correlations and does not experimentally modify the epigenome, so it only partially supports the causal wording of the claim.
This review discusses DNA methylation and healthy human aging in general terms. It does not address brain-specific epigenetic changes or genes related to neurogenesis.

assessments.explanation: Human temporal neocortex study (125 subjects, 17 weeks gestation to 104 years) showing age-related DNA methylation changes at 50 CNS-related loci, including neurogenesis-related NEUROD1 and NEUROD2 (sentence 3). These are correlational age-associated changes. The abstract does not test modifying the brain epigenome or show that such modification affects the aging process, so the causal part of the claim is not addressed.

Review article proposing that age-dependent epigenomic and chromatin changes contribute to aging in general. It does not specify the brain, human subjects, or neurogenesis-related genes, and it reports no intervention on the brain epigenome. It is too general to support or contradict the brain-specific, neurogenesis-gene claim.

Study in mice on hippocampal neural stem cells and Notch signaling. It reports reduced neurogenesis in aged mice and reversible quiescence, but it does not study the human aging process or any epigenomic modification. Animal findings do not establish the human claim.
